name: LLM-guided evolutionary program search
summary: An LLM proposes edits to code, an automated evaluator scores each candidate, and an evolutionary database keeps the best and most diverse programs, finding heuristics and constructions that beat human-designed ones.
mechanism: A human supplies a program skeleton, the part to evolve (one priority function in FunSearch; arbitrary blocks across a file in AlphaEvolve), and an evaluator that runs a candidate and returns scores. A programs database holds evaluated programs; samplers build prompts from high-scoring and diverse parents and ask an LLM for a modified program; evaluators execute and score it; results flow back into the database. Diversity is kept with island populations (FunSearch) or MAP-Elites grids (OpenEvolve). Samplers and evaluators run asynchronously in parallel. The output is readable source code, so a discovered heuristic can be inspected, tested and shipped like hand-written code.
limitations: Requires a fast, automatic, trustworthy evaluator; anything judged by taste or fun has no such evaluator, and evolved code overfits whatever the evaluator measures.;Each run consumes thousands of LLM samples and program executions in earlier systems; ShinkaEvolve's roughly 150-sample result shows efficiency varies widely by problem.;Evolved heuristics are tuned to the benchmark instances and must be re-validated on new maps, content or patches.;No game studio use was found in this run's sources; all cited results are in mathematics, scheduling and systems code.

name: Agent-based automated playtesting and balancing
aliases: RL playtesting;human-like playtesting;difficulty prediction agents;game testing agents
summary: Studios train imitation, reinforcement learning, and search agents to play builds, estimating level difficulty, pass and churn rates, progression pacing, map coverage, and exploits before players reach them.
mechanism: Agents play the game through an API or the rendered screen, in three families. Human-like agents are trained by supervised imitation of logged player moves, as with King's CNN on Candy Crush data, and their success rate on a new level predicts its difficulty for people. Goal-driven search or RL agents (A*, evolution strategies, deep RL) optimize task completion, and their action counts and success rates measure progression balance, as in EA's career-balancing study for The Sims Mobile. Curiosity agents are rewarded for novel states, maximizing map coverage to find stuck spots, missing collision, and unintended shortcuts. Agent results can feed a model of the player population: Roohi et al. combined RL agent pass rates with simulated skill, persistence, and boredom to predict per-level churn. In production, agents run against new builds inside the existing test pipeline and their coverage and failures are visualized for designers.
limitations: Agents are not players: skill and style differ, and imitation agents need large logs of real player moves, which a new game lacks before launch.;Integration dominates cost: EA SEED found engineering RL into production builds was the largest time sink, partly because development builds differ from the shipped game.;Deep RL transfers poorly between games without heavy hyperparameter tuning, so cost grows roughly linearly with the number of titles.;Open-ended simulation games have no single goal to optimize, so coverage or curiosity rewards stand in for design intent and can miss balance problems that only appear over long play.

name: Automated generation of game rules and mechanics
summary: Systems that write complete game rule sets as code in a description language, using evolution or language models to propose rules and self-play agents to score balance, decisiveness, and strategic depth before a human sees them.
mechanism: Rules are written in a game description language. Ludii describes a game as a tree of ludemes (board, pieces, moves, end conditions) that compiles to a playable game; VGDL describes sprites, interactions, and termination for 2D video games. A generator proposes new rule trees: Browne and Maire's system evolved them by crossover and mutation, while GAVEL fine-tunes CodeLlama-13b with a fill-in-the-middle objective on 574 Ludii games and uses it as the mutation operator in MAP-Elites: a span of an existing game's rule code is masked and the model writes a replacement, and the archive is indexed by a 2D PCA projection of 510 Ludii concept features (1,600 cells). Candidates pass hierarchical tests (compiles, is playable, random playouts are not trivially one-sided and offer real choices) and are then scored by MCTS self-play on balance, decisiveness, completion, agency, coverage, and strategic depth. LLM frameworks built on VGDL generate rules and levels together from prompts. The output is a set of verified candidate rule sets for designers to play and select.
limitations: Generated rule sets are small abstract board games; GAVEL trained on 574 games after removing those over 1,024 tokens, far below the size of a simulation game's rule base.;Self-play metrics such as balance, decisiveness, and agency describe agent play, not whether people enjoy the game, so human evaluation is still required.;Every candidate needs compilation plus random and MCTS playouts, so the search is offline and compute-bound.;Language models often emit rule code that fails to compile or is unplayable; GAVEL penalizes such candidates rather than preventing them.;Simulation games rarely have a formal rule language like Ludii or VGDL, so applying this needs the game's systems exposed as data or a scripting layer the generator can edit.

name: Language models grounded in strategic planning for negotiation games
summary: Meta's Cicero couples a dialogue language model with a planning engine that infers other players' intentions from the board and conversation, so its free-text negotiation proposes and follows concrete joint plans, reaching human-level Diplomacy.
mechanism: Each phase, a planning module predicts every player's likely actions from the board state and the dialogue so far. It starts from a policy model trained on human games and refines it with piKL, a regret-minimization search regularized by a KL penalty toward the human-like policy, so predictions stay plausible while improving expected value. The resulting plan fixes intents: the actions Cicero intends to take and the actions it proposes to each recipient. A dialogue language model, trained on human game messages and conditioned on the board, the message history, and these intents, generates candidate messages, which are filtered for consistency with the plan and the game state. Incoming messages update the predicted intents of others, which changes the plan and therefore what Cicero says next. The planner also models what others expect Cicero to do. Because messages are generated from intents rather than freely, what Cicero says tracks what it plans to do.
limitations: Built for one game: the dialogue model and the move policy were trained on human Diplomacy games and messages, so another game needs comparable data or a substitute.;Released weights are licensed for non-commercial use only (CC-BY-NC 4.0), and the repository is archived, so a studio cannot ship the released model.;Training assumed a GPU cluster (example 256 GPUs) and inference loads large models per agent, which is costly for a game with several AI factions per player.;Evaluation used an anonymous league; how players negotiate and whether they trust an opponent they know is an AI was not measured.

name: Grammar-constrained decoding for valid game actions
summary: Decoding that masks every token which cannot extend a valid string of a schema, regular expression, or grammar, so a model's output always parses as a legal game action or data record.
mechanism: The output format (a JSON Schema, regular expression, or context-free grammar) is compiled into an automaton. At each decoding step the engine computes which vocabulary tokens keep the partial output a valid prefix and sets the logits of all others to minus infinity before sampling. Outlines precomputes an index from finite-state-machine states to allowed tokens; XGrammar handles full CFGs by prechecking context-independent tokens and checking context-dependent ones with a persistent stack, overlapping grammar work with GPU execution; hosted APIs convert schemas to CFGs and cache them; llama.cpp accepts GBNF grammars for local models. For games, the schema is built from current state: an enum of legal verbs, target ids that exist, and numeric fields with bounds, so every output maps to an action the engine can execute. A simpler variant scores a fixed list of candidate actions and returns the chosen index.
limitations: Validity is not correctness: a well-formed action can still be the wrong action or reference stale state, so engines must re-check preconditions.;Format constraints can lower reasoning quality; a common workaround is free-form reasoning followed by a constrained final answer, which costs tokens.;Schema coverage varies: hosted APIs support a JSON Schema subset, and llama.cpp silently skips unsupported features such as nested $ref and uniqueItems and slows down with many optional items.;First use of a new schema adds compile latency (OpenAI reports under 10 seconds, up to a minute), so per-turn dynamic schemas need caching.;Output can still fail validation if generation hits a token limit.

name: Continuous cellular automata and foundation-model search for artificial life
summary: Continuous cellular automata such as Lenia and mass-conserving Flow-Lenia produce lifelike self-organizing creatures, and ASAL uses vision-language foundation models to search their rule spaces for phenomena described in text or for open-ended novelty.
mechanism: Lenia stores a continuous field A(x) in [0,1]. Each step it convolves A with a smooth ring-shaped kernel K, passes the result through a bell-shaped growth function G, and updates A by a small time step dt times G(K*A), clipped to [0,1]; certain kernel and growth parameters yield moving, self-maintaining patterns ('species'). Flow-Lenia replaces additive growth with an affinity field that moves matter along its gradient, conserving total mass, and stores the rule parameters in the matter itself, so creatures carrying different rules can coexist, collide and mix. ASAL renders a simulation, embeds the frames with a vision-language foundation model, and scores parameter sets by similarity to a text prompt, by novelty of the embedding trajectory over time, or by diversity across a population; an evolutionary optimizer then searches the substrate's parameters (Boids, Particle Life, Game of Life, Lenia, NCA).
limitations: Lenia creatures exist in a narrow band of parameter space; most settings die out or explode, which is what made search tools necessary.;Creatures are fields without discrete identity, needs or stats, so connecting them to resource economies or player goals needs extra interpretation layers.;ASAL scores runs with a foundation model on rendered frames, which is offline-scale compute and inherits that model's notion of what looks interesting.;Open-ended evolution in these substrates is a stated aim, not an established result.

name: Deep reinforcement learning policies for NPC opponents and navigation
aliases: Gran Turismo Sophy;GT Sophy;learned NPC controllers;Unity ML-Agents
summary: Neural control policies trained with deep reinforcement learning inside the game's own simulation drive opponents and NPCs, as with Sony AI's Gran Turismo Sophy, a selectable rival in Gran Turismo 7 since 2023.
mechanism: The game exposes observations (car state, track geometry, nearby opponents; or local terrain and goal direction for navigation) and actions (steering, throttle, brake; or movement and ability inputs) to a learning agent. Many instances run in parallel, and model-free deep RL learns a policy network that maps observations to actions to maximize a shaped reward. For GT Sophy the reward values course progress and was designed to encode racing's under-specified sportsmanship rules, and training mixed racing scenarios so one policy handles both speed and tactics. For NPCs with jetpacks, grappling hooks, or double jumps, where navigation meshes break down, the reward is reaching a goal. The trained network is small enough to run every frame. Difficulty is set by giving the agent cars of different performance or alternate checkpoints, and later GT Sophy versions expose settings such as tire and fuel consumption. Toolkits such as Unity ML-Agents connect engine scenes to training code.
limitations: Coverage arrives per content item: GT Sophy grew from four cars and four tracks to nine tracks and 340 cars across updates, because each track and car needs training and validation.;A policy trained to win needs reward shaping and later refinement for sportsmanship and enjoyment; Sony AI describes refining GT Sophy's behavior for etiquette and players of all skill levels after the research version.;Availability was narrow at first: GT Sophy 2.0 ran only in Quick Race on PS5, not in other events on the same tracks.;Learned policies are hard to direct for scripted moments, and physics or content patches can require retraining and re-validation.;Deep RL transfers poorly between games without heavy tuning, as EA reported, so each title builds its own training setup.

name: Differentiable simulation
summary: Simulators written so automatic differentiation returns gradients of an outcome with respect to initial state, controls, or rule parameters, replacing black-box search with gradient descent for tuning and inverse design.
mechanism: The simulator step is written in a language with automatic differentiation: source-transformed kernels (DiffTaichi, NVIDIA Warp) or traced array programs (JAX in Brax). A loss is defined on the final or accumulated state, for example distance of a soft robot from a goal or error between simulated and observed infection counts. Reverse-mode differentiation propagates the gradient back through every timestep to the parameters, which are updated by gradient descent. Contacts and discrete events are smoothed or given surrogate gradients. For agent-based models, agent state is held in tensors and stochastic discrete events are replaced by differentiable relaxations so the whole population update has gradients (GradABM). The payoff is that tuning takes tens of gradient iterations instead of thousands of blind rollouts.
limitations: Collisions, contact switching, and integer or threshold game rules give zero, undefined, or misleading gradients and need smoothing or relaxations that change the dynamics being tuned.;Reverse-mode differentiation must store or recompute intermediate states, so memory grows with timesteps times state size; long horizons also produce exploding or vanishing gradients.;Support is incomplete in production-grade GPU engines; MuJoCo Warp lists differentiability via Warp as not yet available.;Gradient descent finds local optima of a stated loss; matching a target curve is not the same as making a system fun or balanced.

name: Diffusion and autoregressive neural game engines
summary: Action-conditioned generative models trained on recordings of one existing game predict each next frame from recent frames and player input, so the model itself plays the role of the game engine.
mechanism: A game is recorded as pairs of frames and player actions (from an RL agent in GameNGen, human play in DIAMOND's CS:GO model, or gameplay video in Oasis). A generator is trained to predict frame t+1 from the last N frames and the action at t: a latent diffusion model in GameNGen, DIAMOND, and Oasis, or a transformer over interleaved image and action tokens in MineWorld. Context frames are noised during training (noise augmentation, Diffusion Forcing, dynamic noising) so the model can recover from its own errors during long rollouts, and sampling is cut to a few denoising steps for real-time play. There is no explicit game state: position, health, enemies, and map layout exist only as pixels or latents inside the context window, so anything that leaves the window is forgotten unless it is visible on screen.
limitations: Memory is a few seconds: GameNGen's 64-frame context covers about 3 seconds, and Oasis shows about 3 seconds of memory in one example, so off-screen state such as map layout or enemy positions is lost.;Requires an existing game to record: GameNGen needed about 70M agent frames from DOOM, DIAMOND 87 hours of CS:GO play; the approach clones a game rather than authoring a new one.;Each player needs a dedicated accelerator (one TPU-v5 for GameNGen, H100s for Oasis); Maginative reports cost remains a significant barrier to deploying such models at scale, and no per-player-hour figure is published.;State such as health, ammo, inventory, and score is only as reliable as the pixels that show it; Oasis inventory control is imprecise and distant geometry is fuzzy.;Training on footage of commercial games raises unresolved licensing questions.

name: 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Scenes are represented as millions of anisotropic 3D Gaussians optimized from photos and rasterized in real time, giving photoreal captured or generated environments at 1080p and 30+ fps.
mechanism: Starting from sparse structure-from-motion points, each Gaussian stores position, anisotropic covariance, opacity, and view-dependent color as spherical harmonics. A differentiable tile-based rasterizer projects, depth-sorts, and alpha-blends the Gaussians; gradients from photo reconstruction error update parameters while adaptive density control splits, clones, and prunes Gaussians. Rendering needs no neural network at runtime, so it runs at real-time rates. Extensions attach physics directly to the Gaussians (PhysGaussian runs a Material Point Method on the kernels), stream level-of-detail on the web, and standardize the format in glTF.
limitations: Colors store captured radiance, so lighting is baked in; dynamic time of day, player-placed lights, and relighting are not supported by the base method.;Memory heavy: millions of Gaussians per scene and training peaks above 20 GB.;No collision geometry or semantics: gameplay needs separate meshes or proxies for physics and pathfinding.;Editing and stylizing splats is harder than editing meshes; tooling and a ratified interchange standard were still arriving in 2026.

name: Generalist instructable game agents (SIMA)
summary: Agents that read screen pixels and natural-language instructions and output keyboard and mouse actions across many commercial 3D games, with later versions reasoning, conversing, and improving through self-generated tasks.
mechanism: The agent sees only rendered frames and a language instruction and emits keyboard and mouse actions in real time, with no access to game source, state APIs, or per-game reward code. SIMA (2024) was trained on human gameplay with language annotations across nine commercial games and four research environments covering about 600 short skills (navigate, interact with objects, use menus). SIMA 2 (2025) puts a fine-tuned Gemini Flash-Lite model at the core, so the agent reasons about goals, states its plan, converses, and follows sketches or emoji. It then improves without human data: a Gemini task setter proposes tasks likely achievable from the current state, the agent attempts them, a Gemini reward model scores each trajectory from 0 to 100 (50 or more counts as success), and the agent trains on the scored experience.
limitations: Weak combat and precise low-level control; failures in held-out games are often due to poor exploration.;Short memory bounded by the context window, and trouble with long multi-step tasks that need goal verification.;Built on Gemini Flash-Lite for latency; fine-tuning cost general reasoning (about 25.5% drop on AIME after SFT).;Runs as a cloud model reading the screen, so per-session inference cost and round-trip latency apply; no public cost figures.;Not available to players; the reward model was calibrated on a small set of trajectories.

name: Prompt-to-persistent 3D world generation
summary: Models such as World Labs Marble and HunyuanWorld turn text, images, video, or coarse 3D blockouts into persistent explorable scenes exported as Gaussian splats and meshes with collision proxies.
mechanism: An image or video diffusion model generates views of a scene (a 360-degree panorama in HunyuanWorld, multi-view images in Marble) from the prompt; the views are lifted to an explicit 3D representation (3D Gaussian splats, or a semantically layered mesh) that can be walked through and re-rendered without regeneration. Marble also emits triangle meshes and coarse collider meshes for physics, can expand or merge worlds, and in Chisel mode takes a blockout of boxes and planes as structure and a text prompt as style. A parallel line renders frames directly instead of building geometry: RTFM keeps generated frames with camera poses as spatial memory and retrieves nearby frames as context. Atlas (2026) is a multimodal model that outputs video, point clouds, and splats.
limitations: Scenes are static: no dynamic objects, agents, or rules are generated, and RTFM lists dynamics and interaction as future work.;Single-image or text prompts force the model to invent unseen regions; Marble notes artifacts and less crisp far regions that expansion may fix.;Splat output bakes lighting into colors, so day-night cycles and relighting need conversion to meshes or other methods.;Collider meshes are coarse and need manual work for gameplay-critical collision.;Corporate change (World Labs joining AMD in 2026) leaves the hosted product's future terms uncertain.

name: Generative agents (memory stream, reflection, planning)
summary: LLM-driven characters that store observations in a natural-language memory stream, retrieve them by recency, importance, and relevance, synthesize reflections, and plan their day top-down.
mechanism: Each agent appends observations as natural-language records to a memory stream. To act or speak, it retrieves records by a score that sums min-max normalized recency (exponential decay, factor 0.995 per game hour), importance (an LLM rating from 1 to 10 made when the record is stored), and relevance (embedding cosine similarity to the current situation), all with weight 1. When the summed importance of recent records exceeds 150, roughly two or three times a game day, the agent asks the LLM for high-level questions and inferences and stores the answers as reflections that can be retrieved like observations. Planning is top-down: a daily sketch is decomposed into hour chunks and then 5-15 minute actions, and the plan is revised when a perceived event warrants a reaction. Dialogue is generated from retrieved memories about the other agent. Cost-reduction variants replay stored plan-action sequences when a new plan matches an old one by embedding similarity and compress social context into short summaries, cutting LLM calls.
limitations: Cost and wall-clock time: 25 agents over two game days cost thousands of dollars and took days to run on gpt-3.5-turbo (2023 prices).;Retrieval failures and embellishment: agents sometimes miss relevant memories or add fabricated details to recalled events.;Instruction-tuned models make agents overly formal and cooperative, and agents misread location norms such as single-occupancy bathrooms or closing hours.;Each agent step is several sequential LLM calls (importance rating, retrieval-conditioned action, dialogue, reflection), so per-agent latency is seconds, which limits real-time populations unless calls are cached or batched.;Behavior is not reproducible from a seed with hosted models; replays and saves must store generated outputs.

name: Genie foundation world models
summary: Google DeepMind's Genie models generate playable worlds from a text or image prompt and render them in real time from player input, with Genie 3 reaching 720p at 24 fps and about a minute of visual memory.
mechanism: Genie (2024) learned from 30k hours of unlabeled 2D platformer video: a video tokenizer, a latent action model that infers 8 discrete actions between frames without labels, and a 10.1B-parameter dynamics model that predicts the next frame tokens given an action. Genie 2 (December 2024) is an autoregressive latent diffusion model with a transformer dynamics model that turns a single image into a 3D world controlled by keyboard and mouse. Genie 3 (August 2025) generates frames auto-regressively in real time from a text prompt, keeps visual memory of earlier frames for about a minute so revisited places look the same, and accepts text 'promptable world events' during play that add objects, characters, or weather changes. No explicit 3D scene or game state is stored; consistency comes from the frame history.
limitations: Session length: Genie 2 coherence is usually 10 to 20 seconds; Genie 3 manages a few minutes; Project Genie caps exploration at 60 seconds because of compute.;No inspectable state: there are no variables for inventory, health, or object identity, so mechanics that need stocks or rules must live in a separate system.;Limited action space and no reliable multi-agent interaction (DeepMind's stated Genie 3 limitations).;Access is a hosted research prototype for paying subscribers; no public API, price per hour, or on-device version is published.;Guardrails refuse copyrighted settings and nudity, which constrains user-generated worlds.

name: Graph network simulators and neural operators
aliases: GNS;MeshGraphNets;Fourier Neural Operator;FNO;learned physics simulators;neural PDE surrogates
summary: Learned simulators that predict the next state of particles, meshes, or continuous fields with message-passing networks or Fourier-space operators, trained on numerical solver output and run 10-1000x faster than that solver.
mechanism: Graph network simulators treat particles (GNS) or mesh vertices (MeshGraphNets) as nodes, with edges to neighbors within a radius or along mesh connectivity. An encoder embeds positions, velocities and material type; several rounds of learned message passing compute pairwise interactions; a decoder outputs per-node accelerations that a simple integrator applies. Models are trained on one-step targets from a numerical solver, with noise added to inputs so long rollouts stay stable. MeshGraphNets also learns where to refine the mesh. Neural operators such as the Fourier Neural Operator learn a map from one function to another (for example initial vorticity to vorticity at a later time) by applying learned kernels in Fourier space, so one model covers a family of PDE instances and can be evaluated at grid resolutions not seen in training.
limitations: Errors accumulate over long rollouts; GNS needed training-noise injection to stay stable, and nothing guarantees conservation of mass or energy.;Each material or domain needs a training set generated by a numerical solver, and behavior outside the training distribution (new materials, extreme speeds, novel geometry) is unreliable.;Reported speedups are against the high-accuracy solver used for training, not against the cheap approximations games already ship, so the net gain for a game can be much smaller.;Inference runs on the GPU and competes with rendering for the frame budget.;Results are cited from 2020-2021 primary papers; this run found no shipped game using GNS or neural operators at runtime.

name: LLM models of individual human choice
summary: Language models conditioned on interviews or fine-tuned on millions of experimental choices that predict how specific people or populations answer surveys, play economic games, and choose in decision tasks.
mechanism: Two approaches. Grounded agents put a person's two-hour interview transcript (or survey answers) in the prompt of a generative agent and ask it to answer new questions as that person; accuracy is normalized by how consistently the real person answers the same items two weeks later. Fine-tuned choice models transcribe experiments into natural language and train a model to predict each trial's choice: Centaur adds rank-8 QLoRA adapters (about 0.15% of parameters) to a frozen 4-bit Llama 3.1 70B and trains one epoch on Psych-101 (160 experiments, 60,092 participants, 10,681,650 choices), scoring held-out participants by negative log-likelihood against cognitive models. Earlier silicon-sample work conditions a model on demographic backstories to reproduce subgroup response distributions. In games the same pipeline would predict how players or simulated citizens choose among options described in text.
limitations: Psych-101 is skewed toward WEIRD participants and toward learning and decision-making tasks; individual differences such as age were not in the prompts.;Critics show Centaur performs well even without valid instructions, so its predictions on new game situations may track surface statistics.;Interview-grounded agents need hours of data per person, which raises consent and privacy questions for player data.;Centaur's 70B base needed about five days on one A100 to fine-tune; the 8B Minitaur variant generalized less robustly.;No study yet validates these models on choices inside games, where options are visual, timed, and repeated.

name: Regret minimization and search for imperfect-information games
summary: Self-play algorithms that minimize counterfactual regret over information sets, refined by real-time subgame search, compute hard-to-exploit strategies that bluff and hide information and beat top humans at poker, Stratego, and Scotland Yard.
mechanism: A decision point is an information set: all histories the player cannot tell apart. CFR traverses the game tree repeatedly; at each information set it computes each action's counterfactual regret (how much better it would have done, weighted by the probability that others reach that set) and sets the next strategy by regret matching, proportional to positive cumulative regret. The average strategy converges to a Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum games, and Monte Carlo CFR samples the tree to scale. Large games are abstracted (bucketed hands and bet sizes) into an offline blueprint that is refined during play by subgame search: Libratus used nested subgame solving, DeepStack re-solved to a depth limit with a learned value function, and Pluribus searched a few moves ahead while letting each opponent pick among four continuation strategies at the leaves. ReBeL and Student of Games learn values over public belief states and search with them, reducing to AlphaZero-style search in perfect-information games. DeepNash instead learns a policy model-free with Regularised Nash Dynamics and no search. Outputs are mixed strategies, so the agent bluffs at calibrated rates.
limitations: Convergence guarantees hold for two-player zero-sum games; Pluribus's six-player play works empirically without them, and cooperative or general-sum simulation games fall outside the theory.;Large games need designed abstractions of actions and states; a simulation with continuous economies and many units has no obvious abstraction to solve.;Runtime search costs seconds per decision (Pluribus averaged about 20 seconds per hand on two CPUs), far above per-frame budgets for many agents.;Equilibrium play avoids being exploited rather than exploiting weak players, which can feel passive, and randomized bluffs read as arbitrary unless the game explains them.

name: Learned level and map generation (PCGRL, MarioGPT, LLM generators)
summary: Generators trained by reinforcement learning or on example levels, including small and large language models that emit tile maps from text prompts, produce playable levels and maps without hand-written generation rules.
mechanism: PCGRL treats level design as a sequential decision problem: an agent edits a tile grid step by step (narrow, turtle, or wide representations of where it may edit) and is rewarded by the change in a quality score such as playability, path length, or region count, so the trained generator builds a level in fast forward passes without example levels. ARLPCG adds a solver agent and rewards the generator for levels that are challenging but solvable, with auxiliary control inputs. Language-model generators serialize levels as text and train or prompt a model to continue them: MarioGPT fine-tunes DistilGPT2 with cross-attention to a prompt naming pipes, enemies, blocks, and elevation; Sokoban generators fine-tune on level corpora; Word2World prompts a general LLM to write a story, extract characters and tiles, and place them. Outputs are checked by search agents or solver bots and rejected or repaired if unplayable. Conditional generators such as EA SEED's match-3 cVAE take size, symmetry, and target difficulty as inputs.
limitations: Example data is scarce: MarioGPT trained on 37 levels and LLM Sokoban results scaled with dataset size, so a new game's handful of authored maps may not suffice.;Validity is not guaranteed: about 12% of MarioGPT levels were not completed by an A* agent, so every output needs a solver check.;Conditional control is weak: difficulty conditioning hit its target a third of the time and lowered size and tile-distribution accuracy.;Results are mostly 2D tile grids for small games; large simulation maps with resources, rivers, and settlement suitability carry global constraints these models do not represent.;Training on existing commercial levels such as Super Mario Bros raises IP and platform disclosure questions for shipped use.

name: Learned kinematic motion synthesis
summary: Neural networks generate or compress kinematic character animation, as in Ubisoft's learned motion matching, EA's HyperMotion, and inZOI's motion extraction from uploaded video.
mechanism: Motion matching picks the next pose by searching a database of mocap frames for the best match to a query of current pose and desired trajectory. Learned motion matching replaces the database with three small networks: a Decompressor that maps a feature vector to a full pose, a Stepper that advances features one frame, and a Projector that maps a query to the nearest valid features, giving nearly identical output at constant CPU cost. HyperMotion trains a model on frames of full-team match capture to generate transitions in real time. Video-to-motion tools estimate 3D poses from ordinary video and retarget them onto a game rig. No physics is simulated.
limitations: Kinematic output ignores physics, so characters still clip or float when the environment differs from the training motion.;Learned motion matching saves memory but not per-character CPU time, which still limits crowd counts.;Video-to-motion quality depends on the uploaded footage; occlusion and camera motion produce artifacts that the game must filter or let players discard.

name: Many-agent LLM societies
summary: Simulations of hundreds to a million LLM-driven agents with concurrent cognitive modules, shared environments, and message buses that produce role specialization, rule changes, cultural spread, and polarization.
mechanism: Scaling generative agents from tens to thousands needs architecture and infrastructure changes. Project Sid's PIANO runs about ten modules concurrently (memory, action awareness, goal generation, social awareness, talking, skill execution) that read and write a shared agent state; fast modules use small non-LLM models and slow ones call an LLM, and a cognitive controller acts as a bottleneck that broadcasts one high-level decision so speech and actions stay consistent. AgentSociety gives each agent a profile plus emotion, needs, and cognition layers and simulates mobility, social contact, employment, and consumption across linked urban, social, and economic spaces, distributing agents over Ray processes and routing messages over MQTT. Concordia has agents state intended actions in natural language and a Game Master agent decide outcomes. OASIS runs up to one million agents inside a recommender-driven social feed.
limitations: Scale ceilings come from the host game as well as the model: Project Sid agents became unresponsive above 1,000 agents on a Minecraft server.;PIANO agents lack vision and spatial reasoning and have no innate drives such as survival or curiosity, so building and navigation are weak.;Agents built on pretrained models reproduce known human institutions (taxes, votes, religion) rather than inventing new ones, so outcomes are bounded by training data.;Per-agent LLM calls multiply with population; AgentSociety chose an API without request limits to avoid rate-limit artifacts, and none of these papers reports per-agent-hour cost in a form a game could budget against.;Validation is qualitative (matching stylized findings), so designers cannot easily tune or test collective outcomes.

name: LLM explanation of simulation state
aliases: AI advisor chat;natural-language explanations of agent behavior;LLM commentator;log summarization
summary: Language models that read simulation state, modifier breakdowns, agent traces, or event logs and answer why and what-if questions or summarize what happened for players and designers.
mechanism: The game serializes the relevant slice of state (indicator values and their contributing modifiers, an agent's thought log and action trace, recent events) into the prompt, or exposes it through retrieval or tool calls over game data and documentation, and the model answers a player question or writes a summary. Zhang et al. first learn a compact representation of an agent's behavior from observed states and actions, then have the LLM explain from that representation, which limits hallucination and supports follow-up and what-if questions. For designers, a model can segment play logs into strategies and merge them into a graph to compare with the intended path. The explanation layer reads state and does not write it, so the simulation stays deterministic.
limitations: Wrong but fluent causes: models are unreliable at inferring dynamics, so explanations are only trustworthy when causes are passed in from the simulation.;Serializing large state (thousands of modifiers, long logs) into context is slow and costly; selection of what to include determines what can be explained.;Hard to QA: the answer space is open-ended, and a confident wrong explanation damages trust more than no explanation.;Shipped evidence is thin: known game examples are tech demos or research previews.

name: LLM game master and narrative director
aliases: AI game master;AI Dungeon;Concordia Game Master;story engine;AI narrator
summary: A language model that adjudicates player and NPC intentions, decides outcomes, generates events and quests, and narrates them, either free-form or checked against a typed world state and canon.
mechanism: The player types an intent; the system assembles a prompt from recent story, pinned memories, and setting notes and asks the model to continue the story, as AI Dungeon has since 2019. Grounded variants split the job: actors state intended actions in language, a Game Master component checks plausibility against rules and state, decides what happens, writes state changes, and only then narrates (Concordia). Hidden Door runs intent through plan, canon check, and world-state update steps over a typed, auditable world model, using many small tuned models for about 100 narrative tasks; its example blocks Dracula from entering a house uninvited. Research systems generate setting, items, and NPCs from designer criteria and use the model to validate free-text input against the story (PANGeA), or assist a human Dungeon Master (CALYPSO).
limitations: Long-session consistency: models forget or contradict earlier facts unless state is externalized into memory or a typed world model.;Accommodation bias: models rarely say no, which removes challenge and lets players talk past any obstacle.;Content moderation is hard: AI Dungeon's filter both missed and over-blocked, and Steam requires guardrail disclosure for live-generated content.;Latency of several to 15 seconds per turn frustrated players in a GPT-4 study; multi-step grounded pipelines add calls per turn.;Every turn is an inference cost for the life of the service, which pushes products to subscriptions or small tuned models.

name: LLM-adjudicated state transitions (LLM as game mechanic)
aliases: LLM as rules engine;open-ended combination;text world simulator;memoized generation
summary: A language model computes the outcome of an interaction (two elements combined, an action on an object) from a text description of the inputs, with results cached so every player sees the same rule.
mechanism: The game describes the inputs (two items, or an object state plus an action) as text and asks the model for the result, constrained to a short name, an icon, or a small state diff. Infinite Craft first looks the pair up in a database; only a never-tried pair goes to the model (Llama 2, later Llama 3.1), and the answer is stored, so the rule becomes fixed and shared by all players after the first query and the first finder is credited. The cache turns a stochastic model into a growing deterministic rule table and bounds cost to unique queries. Benchmarks of LLMs as text world simulators measure how often the predicted next state matches the true one.
limitations: Accuracy: as a general state simulator GPT-4 is right on whole-state transitions at most 59.9% of the time, so errors compound over multi-step dynamics.;Legibility: generated rules follow word association rather than a learnable system, so players cannot predict outcomes from principles.;Cost and load scale with unique queries; Infinite Craft's traffic overloaded its servers.;Outputs must be filtered for offensive results because every cached answer becomes permanent shared content.

name: Massively parallel GPU simulation
summary: Simulators that keep thousands of world instances as tensors on a GPU or TPU and step them all in one kernel, raising throughput to millions of steps per second for agent training and Monte Carlo sweeps.
mechanism: World state for N independent instances is stored as structure-of-arrays tensors in accelerator memory. Each tick launches one set of kernels that integrates physics, evaluates game logic, and computes observations and rewards for every instance at once, so policy inference and training read the state without CPU-GPU copies. Implementations compile the step function: JAX/XLA (Brax, MJX, Craftax), CUDA kernels written in Python (NVIDIA Warp, MuJoCo Warp), or a GPU entity-component-system with a task graph (Madrona, where game logic is C++ compiled to CUDA). Throughput comes from parallelism across worlds, not from making one world faster, so the main uses are reinforcement learning (billions of steps), parameter sweeps, and evaluating many randomized variants of one design.
limitations: Speedups come from running many independent worlds in parallel; a single large coupled world, such as one city, gains much less and per-world latency does not improve.;Game logic must be rewritten in a GPU-friendly form (JAX in Craftax, C++ compiled to CUDA in GPUDrive and Madrona), which is a port rather than a recompile.;Madrona requires all component archetypes to be declared up front and does not support adding or removing components at runtime; it is labeled research code with breaking API changes.;Headline frame rates are for simple scenes; contact-rich and dexterous scenes remain hard and much slower (reported caveat on Genesis).;Much of the stack is NVIDIA-specific: MuJoCo Warp needs an NVIDIA GPU for speed, and porting PhysX's 500+ CUDA kernels to other vendors is described as a lot of work.;Policies trained in a batched simulator exploit its physics quirks, so behavior must be re-validated in the shipping engine if that engine differs.

name: Mean field games and mean-field learning
aliases: MFG;mean field MARL;online mirror descent for MFGs
summary: Mean field game theory replaces an N-player game with one representative agent responding to the population distribution, and recent learning methods compute these equilibria for state spaces of hundreds of billions of states.
mechanism: Each agent is small, anonymous and interchangeable, so the game depends on others only through the population distribution m(t,x). An equilibrium is a fixed point: the representative agent's value function u solves a backward Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation given m, and m evolves forward by a Fokker-Planck equation under the resulting policy. Numerical and learning methods iterate this pair: fictitious play averages past best responses; online mirror descent accumulates Q-values and updates the policy by a softmax of them; RL variants learn from samples when the model is unknown. Mean-field multi-agent RL applies the same idea locally, with each agent learning against the mean action of its neighbors. Cost scales with the size of the individual state space, not with the number of agents.
limitations: Assumes anonymous, symmetric, individually negligible agents; named characters with unique state, or a player large enough to move the aggregate, need major-player extensions.;Equilibrium describes settled behavior; the learning, overshoot and panic dynamics games often want are absent unless modeled separately.;The forward-backward coupling needs the whole horizon at once, so player interventions mid-run require re-solving or a fast approximate solver.;Convergence guarantees such as those for online mirror descent need monotonicity assumptions that game rules can violate.;No game implementation was found in this run's sources.

name: Machine-learned weather forecasting
summary: Neural networks trained on decades of atmospheric reanalysis forecast global weather 10-15 days ahead in seconds to minutes on one accelerator, matching or beating physics-based operational models on most verification targets.
mechanism: Models take the current and recent atmospheric state on a global 0.25 degree latitude-longitude grid (temperature, wind, humidity, pressure at many levels plus surface variables) and predict the state one fixed step later; rolling the prediction forward gives a 10-15 day forecast. GraphCast maps grid cells onto a multi-resolution icosahedral mesh and runs learned message passing there. GenCast is a conditional diffusion model that samples stochastic trajectories in 12-hour steps, so repeated samples form an ensemble with calibrated spread. FGN (2025) builds ensembles from learned model perturbations trained on CRPS. Aurora is a 1.3B-parameter foundation model pretrained on over a million hours of geophysical data and fine-tuned for air quality, ocean waves, cyclone tracks and 0.1 degree weather. Inference replaces hours on a supercomputer with seconds to minutes on one accelerator.
limitations: Trained on Earth's reanalysis record, so they reproduce Earth's atmosphere only; fictional planets, altered geography or deliberate climate change lie outside the training data.;Grids are coarse for game maps: 0.25 degree (about 28 km at the equator), and operational AIFS runs at 28 km.;Inference needs an accelerator and gigabytes of weights (Aurora has 1.3B parameters), heavy for client-side use.;Designers cannot author dramatic timing; the model follows the statistics of real weather, so pacing must be imposed by selecting or conditioning forecasts.;Autoregressive rollouts are validated to 10-15 days; behavior over seasons or years is not established by these sources.

name: Self-play planning with learned models (AlphaZero, MuZero, Dreamer)
summary: Agents that combine tree search or imagined rollouts with neural policy and value networks trained by self-play, where MuZero and Dreamer also learn the environment's dynamics, reach superhuman play from rules or pixels alone.
mechanism: AlphaZero pairs MCTS with a network that outputs a move prior p and a value v for a state; games generated by the search train p toward search visit counts and v toward outcomes, so search and network improve each other given only the rules. MuZero drops the need for rules at planning time: a representation network encodes observations into a latent state, a dynamics network predicts the next latent state and reward for an action, and a prediction network outputs policy and value, so MCTS runs entirely in the learned latent space. EfficientZero adds self-supervised consistency and value-prefix losses for sample efficiency. Dreamer learns a recurrent world model and trains an actor-critic on imagined trajectories; DreamerV3 adds symlog and return normalization so one hyperparameter set works across domains, and Dreamer 4 trains its world model mostly on unlabeled video and learns the policy offline inside it. For design work the same loop can be retrained on each rule variant and the converged play compared.
limitations: Training is expensive: MuZero's board-game runs used 16 TPUs for training and 1,000 for self-play, and each significant rule change needs retraining or fine-tuning.;Self-play converges to strong play, not human play, so balance conclusions can reflect exploits humans would never find or use.;Learned dynamics drift over long rollouts; MuZero did poorly on 6 Atari games and DreamerV3 needed about 30M steps (17 days of play) for its first Minecraft diamond.;Most simulation games are many-player, simultaneous-move, partly hidden, and long-horizon, which the two-player perfect-information AlphaZero setup does not cover directly.;Policies are opaque, so designers cannot read why an AI rival chose a strategy, and giving it a personality requires reward shaping rather than editing rules.

name: Monte Carlo tree search for game AI
summary: A best-first search that grows a game tree from repeated simulated playouts and picks branches with a bandit rule such as UCT, letting AI players plan from a forward model without a hand-tuned evaluation function.
mechanism: Each iteration has four steps. Selection descends from the root by a tree policy; UCT picks the child that maximizes mean reward plus c*sqrt(ln N / n), trading exploitation against exploration. Expansion adds an untried child. Simulation plays forward from that node with a cheap default policy (random or heuristic) to a terminal state or depth limit. Backpropagation adds the outcome to the visit count and value of every node on the path. The search is anytime: it stops after an iteration count or time budget and returns the most-visited action. It needs only a forward model that can copy a state, list legal actions, and apply them, so it works for rule sets without a known evaluation function. Variants add chance nodes, determinization or information-set trees for hidden information, simultaneous moves, and macro-actions that search over plans instead of single moves.
limitations: Needs a fast, copyable forward model; a full simulation state with thousands of agents is expensive to clone and step, so practical use usually requires an abstracted model or macro-actions.;Random playouts estimate value poorly in long-horizon systems with delayed consequences such as economies and colony survival unless a heuristic rollout policy or evaluation function is supplied.;Time-budgeted search returns different moves on different hardware, which breaks replays and lockstep multiplayer unless budgets are counted in iterations with seeded randomness.;Determinized search over hidden information averages over sampled worlds and can make choices that are only good if it could see the hidden state (strategy fusion).

name: Muse World and Human Action Model (WHAM)
summary: Microsoft Research's WHAM is a transformer trained on seven years of Bleeding Edge play that generates both future frames and the player's controller actions, aimed at gameplay ideation, with a real-time Quake II follow-up (WHAMM).
mechanism: Frames are encoded into discrete image tokens and controller inputs into action tokens; a decoder-only transformer models the interleaved sequence, so it predicts both how the world evolves and what a human player is likely to do next. Prompting with a few frames yields many plausible continuations (diversity); a designer can edit a frame, such as inserting a character, and the model carries the edit forward (persistency). WHAM-1.6B produces about one frame per second at 300x180. WHAMM replaces token-by-token decoding with MaskGIT-style parallel prediction (a 500M backbone plus a 250M refiner) to reach more than 10 fps at 640x360 on Quake II.
limitations: WHAM-1.6B generates about one image per second at 300x180, too slow and too small for play; WHAMM trades data scope (one level section) for speed.;Needs years of recorded human play with consent terms for a single game; few studios hold such datasets.;Context of under a second (WHAMM) means objects out of view are forgotten.;Counts, damage, and other exact quantities are unreliable in generated frames.

name: Neural cellular automata
aliases: NCA;Growing NCA;DiffLogic CA;differentiable logic cellular automata;self-organising textures
summary: Cellular automata whose local update rule is a small learned network or logic circuit, trained so that cells grow, maintain, and regenerate a target pattern, texture, structure, or level from a seed.
mechanism: Each grid cell holds a state vector (16 channels in Growing NCA: RGB, an alpha channel that marks living cells, and hidden signaling channels). Every step a cell perceives its 3x3 neighborhood through fixed Sobel gradient filters, a shared network of about 8,000 parameters maps the perception vector to a state increment, and a random mask applies the update to roughly half the cells, so no global clock is needed. Cells with no living neighbor are zeroed. The rule is trained by backpropagating through many steps toward a target image or style, with damaged samples in the training pool to teach regeneration. Variants use 3D convolutions for voxel structures, quality-diversity search instead of gradients for game levels, or differentiable logic gates that compile to a discrete binary circuit (DiffLogic CA).
limitations: Each trained rule targets one pattern, texture or structure family; changing the target requires retraining.;Growth unfolds over many steps, so getting a stable result has a latency that instant procedural methods do not have.;Learned rules are opaque to designers and players, apart from small logic-gate circuits, which makes failures hard to diagnose.;Demonstrations are small 2D images, 3D structures of a few thousand blocks, and simple tile domains; robustness under player interference at game scale is not shown.

name: Neural rendering in the graphics pipeline
aliases: DLSS;DLSS 4;DLSS 5;neural shaders;RTX Neural Materials;neural texture compression;neural radiance cache
summary: Small neural networks inside the renderer upscale frames, generate extra frames, denoise ray tracing, decode compressed textures and layered materials, and since DLSS 5 re-light the final frame, all without touching simulation state.
mechanism: DLSS Super Resolution reconstructs a high-resolution frame from a lower-resolution render plus motion vectors with a transformer network (from DLSS 4); Multi Frame Generation predicts up to three (DLSS 4) or five (DLSS 4.5) frames between rendered frames; Ray Reconstruction replaces hand-tuned denoisers. Neural shaders embed small MLPs inside shader code and run them on tensor units: neural texture compression decodes textures from learned latents, neural materials evaluate layered BRDFs, and the neural radiance cache learns multi-bounce indirect light online. DirectX cooperative vectors expose this to cross-vendor shaders. DLSS 5 adds a final network pass that adds lighting and material detail from color and motion vectors, with developer intensity controls and masks.
limitations: Changes presentation, not simulation: CPU-bound simulation games (agent counts, pathfinding, economy ticks) gain nothing from GPU-side neural rendering.;Frame generation adds input latency and artifacts; DLSS 5's final pass reportedly costs 50 to 60 percent of frame rate and can alter art direction.;Hardware-gated: Multi Frame Generation and DLSS 5 require RTX 50-series GPUs at launch, and neural shader features depend on vendor SDKs and cooperative vector support.

name: On-device small language models for characters
aliases: NVIDIA ACE;Smart Zoi;PUBG Ally;co-playable characters;SLM NPCs;quantized local LLMs
summary: Pruned, distilled, and 4-bit quantized language, speech, and embedding models that run on the player's GPU beside rendering to drive character decisions, dialogue, and voice without per-token server cost.
mechanism: A 12B or 8B model is pruned in depth and width and distilled into an 8B, 4B, or 2B student (Minitron), then weights are quantized to 3-4 bits with second-order (GPTQ) or activation-aware (AWQ) methods, shrinking memory so a 2B model fits in about 1.5 GB of VRAM. An in-game inference SDK runs the models in-process and schedules them alongside graphics on the same GPU. A character loop chains on-device speech recognition, the small model (perceive, decide, act, reflect), text-to-speech, and facial animation, with an in-process embedding model for memory retrieval; slow strategic planning can be offloaded to a larger cloud model while fast decisions stay local. Fine-tuning a small model on a narrow game task can beat much larger general models on that task.
limitations: Hardware floor: the inference SDK needs an RTX 30-series class GPU with 8 GB of VRAM minimum, which excludes many players and consoles, and the model competes with rendering for VRAM and GPU time.;Small models are less capable at multi-step reasoning, so vendors offload strategic planning to cloud models, reintroducing cost and latency.;Quality and safety filters must also run locally; local weights can be extracted or modified by players.;Player reception risk: inZOI drew negative user reviews in May 2025 after Krafton announced its generative AI use.;Exact model sizes and latency in shipped titles are mostly undisclosed.

name: Open-ended co-generation of environments and agents
summary: Systems that keep generating new environments or tasks at the edge of an agent's ability and train agents on them, from POET's co-evolved terrains to OMNI-EPIC's foundation-model-written task code and SIMA 2 practicing in Genie 3 worlds.
mechanism: POET keeps a population of environment-agent pairs. It mutates environment parameters (for a 2D walker: roughness, gap width, stump height), admits a child environment only if current agents score within a band that is neither too easy nor too hard, optimizes each agent in its paired environment, and periodically tests whether an agent from another pair does better there, transferring it if so. Enhanced POET adds a novelty measure based on how agents rank on an environment and a more flexible environment encoding. OMNI-EPIC replaces parameter mutation with a foundation model that writes environment and reward code for a physics simulator, conditioned on an archive of solved and failed tasks; a model of interestingness rejects near-duplicates, an RL agent trains on each task, and a success check decides whether the task enters the archive. SIMA 2 has Gemini propose tasks and estimate rewards in commercial games and in Genie 3 generated worlds, then trains later agents on its own experience. The shared loop is: generate a task, check it is learnable, train, archive, repeat.
limitations: Cost is dominated by training or evaluating an agent on every candidate task, so the loop runs offline and is too slow to respond to a live player directly.;Interestingness and success are judged by foundation models or generated code that can be wrong, and generated reward code can be satisfied by unintended behavior.;SIMA 2 still struggles with very long-horizon tasks, short memory, precise low-level control, and robust visual understanding, which limits the tasks it can practice.;Worlds generated by video world models are approximate and short-horizon rather than rules-exact simulations, so success checks inside them are approximate.

name: Open real-time interactive video world models
summary: Open and startup interactive video models (Matrix-Game, Hunyuan-GameCraft, WorldPlay, Yan, Mirage, Odyssey) adapt pretrained video diffusion transformers to keyboard and mouse control and stream frames in real time, adding pose-indexed memory and text edits during play.
mechanism: A pretrained text- or image-to-video diffusion transformer (SkyReels-V2 for Matrix-Game 2.0, HunyuanVideo for GameCraft) gets action modules: keyboard and mouse mapped to camera translation and rotation, injected through cross-attention, token addition, or Plucker camera embeddings. Training uses gameplay recordings from Unreal Engine scenes, GTA V, Minecraft, Temple Run, or 100+ AAA titles. The bidirectional model is then distilled into a causal few-step generator (Self-Forcing with distribution matching, or phased consistency models) that streams chunks with a rolling KV cache. 2026 systems add memory by retrieving past frames whose camera pose overlaps the current view (Matrix-Game 3.0, WorldPlay). Yan, Mirage 2, and Odyssey-2 accept typed text during play to edit the world.
limitations: Resolution and speed trade against hardware: Matrix-Game 2.0 is 352x640 on one H100, Matrix-Game 3.0's 720p 40 fps needs 9 GPUs, and GameCraft runs at 6.6 fps after distillation.;Consistency horizon is about a minute even with retrieval memory; earlier open models have no explicit memory at all.;Training data includes recordings of commercial games (GTA V, 100+ AAA titles), so output provenance is contested.;Stronger history conditioning improves consistency but reduces responsiveness to new actions (GameCraft ablation).;Action spaces cover camera movement and basic locomotion; game verbs such as shooting, building, or trading are not modeled.

name: Physical-world foundation models
summary: Video-pretrained models of physical dynamics, NVIDIA Cosmos for generating action-conditioned training video and Meta's V-JEPA 2 for latent prediction and planning, target robotics and driving rather than games.
mechanism: Cosmos curates about 20M hours of raw video into about 100M clips, compresses them with causal video tokenizers, and pretrains diffusion (Text2World, Video2World) and autoregressive world models that developers post-train into action- or camera-conditioned simulators; Cosmos 3 (2026) is an omni family at 4B, 16B, and 64B parameters. V-JEPA 2 instead predicts masked video in a learned embedding space, not pixels, from over 1M hours of video; its action-conditioned variant V-JEPA 2-AC is post-trained on under 62 hours of robot video and plans by searching for action sequences whose predicted embedding approaches a goal image.
limitations: Designed for robots and vehicles; no game integration or game-specific evaluation exists in the cited sources.;Physical plausibility is unreliable: video models are at or near chance on IntPhys 2.;Large models (up to 64B in Cosmos 3) are far from per-player real-time budgets.;V-JEPA 2 predicts at a single time scale, limiting long-horizon planning (Meta's stated limitation).

name: Learned physics-based character control
summary: Neural policies trained with reinforcement learning drive simulated humanoids by joint torques to imitate motion capture, and MaskedMimic-style controllers accept partial goals such as keyframes, text, or an object to sit on.
mechanism: A ragdoll with joint actuators is simulated in a physics engine; a policy network outputs PD targets each step and is trained with RL in massively parallel GPU simulation to track motion capture clips. MaskedMimic first trains a full-body tracker, then distills it into a conditional generative student that receives a masked goal: any subset of future joint positions, a text description, a head and hand signal from VR, a path, or a target object. The same controller therefore handles locomotion, steering, and sitting on varied furniture and transfers flat-ground motions to rough terrain. InterMimic distills per-subject teachers into one student refined by RL for whole-body human-object interaction from imperfect mocap.
limitations: Every character needs a physics simulation step plus policy inference, which is costly at the hundreds-of-agents scale colony and management sims use; no crowd-scale runtime figures are published in the cited work.;Training requires large mocap datasets and GPU-parallel RL; retargeting to non-human or stylized rigs requires retraining.;Physical controllers can fall or jitter in edge cases, which is hard to QA across open-ended situations.

name: Quality-diversity search (MAP-Elites) for content and balance
summary: Evolutionary search that keeps the best solution found in each cell of a grid of designer-chosen behavior descriptors, returning an archive of diverse high-quality levels, decks, or strategies instead of one optimum.
mechanism: The designer picks k behavior descriptors (for a level: enemy count and number of jumps; for a deck: mean mana cost and minion count) and discretizes them into a grid. Each cell stores the highest-fitness solution seen with those descriptor values. Each iteration selects elites from the archive, mutates or recombines them, evaluates the child's fitness and descriptors (usually by simulation or an agent playthrough), and inserts it if its cell is empty or it beats the incumbent. The archive shows which trait combinations can be good and how good. Variants slide cell boundaries to follow where solutions cluster (MESB), search a generative model's latent space with CMA-ES emitters (CMA-ME on a Mario GAN), use a learned surrogate to predict agent behavior and skip simulations (DSAGE), or use language models both to propose variations and to judge quality and diversity (QDAIF). GAVEL applies MAP-Elites to game rule sets.
limitations: Every candidate needs a fitness and descriptor evaluation, usually a simulated playthrough, so large archives cost many simulations; surrogate methods such as DSAGE exist to cut that cost.;Results depend on the chosen descriptors: poor choices give diversity along axes players do not perceive, and the grid grows exponentially with the number of descriptors.;Fitness measured with AI agents reflects agent skill, not human experience, so cells marked playable or balanced may not match player perception.;Game applications in the cited work are research prototypes on small games (Mario levels, Hearthstone decks); no documented shipped use in a simulation game was found in this run.

name: Real-time generative restyling of game video
summary: A live video-to-video diffusion model repaints each frame of a running game from a text prompt in under 40 ms, leaving the game's own simulation and state untouched.
mechanism: The host game renders normally and streams its frames to a video-to-video diffusion model. Each output frame is conditioned on the current input frame, a window of recently generated frames, and a text prompt; Diffusion Forcing and history augmentation keep the stream from drifting, and distillation, pruning, and custom GPU kernels bring response under 40 ms at 24 fps. Because the model only replaces pixels, collision, inventory, and world state stay in the host engine. Decart's Oasis 2.0 packages this as a Minecraft mod with chat commands and command-block hooks that switch the prompt.
limitations: Short frame window and no long-term memory, so restyled objects can change appearance between views.;Rendered detail can contradict game state (a block that looks like a door but is solid), hurting legibility.;Cloud-served stream adds network latency and per-player GPU cost; no price per hour is published.

name: Realtime speech-to-speech and expressive TTS for characters
aliases: speech-to-speech;full-duplex dialogue;Realtime API;Moshi;expressive TTS;AI NPC voices
summary: Streaming speech recognition, speech-native language models, and context-aware text-to-speech that let characters hold spoken, interruptible conversations with roughly 200-250 ms response onset and generated emotional delivery.
mechanism: Two pipelines. Cascaded: streaming speech recognition, then an LLM, then streaming TTS, each optimized for time to first output. Speech-native: the model reads and writes audio tokens from a neural codec. Moshi models the user's and its own speech as parallel streams (full duplex, so it can listen while speaking) and predicts time-aligned text tokens before audio tokens. Hosted realtime APIs keep a persistent WebSocket session with voice activity detection, interruption handling, and function calls that can trigger game actions. Expressive TTS conditions delivery on context: Sesame's CSM feeds prior conversation audio and text to a Llama-style backbone over codec tokens, and Eleven v3 accepts inline tags such as [whispers] or [sighs]. Small ASR and TTS models (hundreds of millions of parameters) can run on device.
limitations: Cost scales with talk time: at 2024 Realtime API rates, an hour split evenly between player and NPC speech is roughly $9 before context re-reads; gpt-realtime rates cut that to roughly $3 (estimates derived from list prices).;Expressive delivery and low latency trade off: context-conditioned prosody still trails humans, and the most expressive TTS was not suited to real time at launch.;Voice actor consent and compensation are now contract terms, and players have penalized AI voices in reviews.;Speech-native models are hard to constrain to game-legal actions; most games keep a text layer between speech and game state.;Microphone use and online connectivity raise privacy and access barriers (Whispers from the Star lists a broadband connection and an account).

name: ML reconstruction of the planet from aerial imagery
summary: Machine learning classifies buildings, vegetation, and terrain in satellite and aerial imagery and procedural rules rebuild them as 3D scenery, which Microsoft Flight Simulator streams for the whole Earth.
mechanism: Models trained on labeled imagery detect buildings, trees, and land cover in satellite and aerial imagery and map data and extrapolate approximate geometry; offline procedural generation then builds and dresses the buildings and places vegetation, while selected cities use photogrammetry meshes. The reconstruction runs offline in the cloud, and the result is streamed to players on demand as they fly, with procedural filling where imagery is poor.
limitations: Accuracy is bounded by imagery quality; blurred or pixelated areas fall back to procedural fill.;Requires cloud streaming of petabyte-scale data and a licensed imagery source.;Reconstructed buildings are generic from inferred class and height, not modeled individually, except in photogrammetry cities.

name: Simulation-based inference for calibrating simulators
summary: Neural density estimators trained on simulator runs return a posterior over a simulator's parameters given observed data, calibrating agent-based and economic models whose likelihoods cannot be computed.
mechanism: Draw parameters theta from a prior, run the simulator to get outputs x, and train a conditional density estimator, usually a normalizing flow, to approximate p(theta | x) from the (theta, x) pairs (neural posterior estimation). Conditioning on observed data x_o gives the posterior; sequential variants such as APT draw new simulations from proposals concentrated near x_o. Related variants learn the likelihood or a likelihood ratio instead. Summary statistics can be hand-chosen or learned, for example with a temporal graph neural network over agent-level microstates. The method needs only forward runs, no likelihood and no gradients, and once trained it is amortized: a new observation gets its posterior in one forward pass.
limitations: Needs many simulator runs, from thousands to hundreds of thousands depending on method and dimensionality, which is costly for slow, full-scale game simulations.;A misspecified simulator yields confident posteriors over wrong parameters; calibration fits the data and does not validate the model.;Posterior quality depends on the summary statistics or learned embeddings of noisy, high-dimensional outputs.;Matching real data or telemetry targets does not make a mechanic fun; it only removes guesswork about parameter values.;No game studio use was found in this run's sources.

name: Subspace neural physics and learned deformers
aliases: Ubisoft subspace neural physics;Unreal ML Deformer;learned cloth deformation;neural morph model
summary: Small networks trained on offline cloth, flesh, or muscle simulation predict deformation in a compressed subspace or as corrective morph targets, running hundreds to thousands of times faster than the source simulation inside a game engine.
mechanism: Developers run an expensive offline simulation (cloth, soft tissue, muscle, volume-preserving flesh) over many randomized poses or interactions. Vertex positions are compressed, for example with principal component analysis, into a low-dimensional subspace. A small network is trained to predict the next subspace coordinates from the current coordinates plus external inputs such as bone transforms or collider positions (Holden et al. 2019), or to predict per-pose corrective morph-target weights applied on top of linear skinning (Unreal Engine ML Deformer, Neural Morph Model and Nearest Neighbor Model). At runtime only the network and the decode from subspace to full mesh run, on the GPU.
limitations: Quality holds only near the training distribution of poses and interactions; unusual poses or collisions produce artifacts, so coverage of the offline dataset sets the limit.;Training is heavy: Unreal's documentation notes long training times and Alembic training caches of 50-100 GB.;GPU memory for morph targets is the main runtime cost, and compression settings trade memory and speed for quality.;Output is usually cosmetic; it does not feed back into gameplay physics unless the game reads the deformed state, which brings determinism and consistency issues.;No commercial title using these models at runtime was confirmed in this run's sources.

name: Text- and image-to-3D asset generation
summary: Open 3D generative models (TRELLIS, Hunyuan3D 2.x, Roblox Cube) produce textured meshes from a text prompt or image in seconds to a minute, and inZOI exposes image-to-3D object creation to players.
mechanism: Generation is split into shape and appearance. A flow-matching or diffusion transformer generates a 3D latent conditioned on an image or text: TRELLIS uses a Structured LATent (sparse voxels carrying features from a vision foundation model), Hunyuan3D-DiT a shape latent, and Roblox Cube discrete shape tokens predicted autoregressively. Decoders turn the latent into meshes, 3D Gaussians, or radiance fields. Texture is painted by a multi-view diffusion model (Hunyuan3D-Paint) or decoded directly, with 2025 versions emitting PBR maps (base color, roughness, metallic). Output is a GLB or OBJ file that drops into an engine like any other asset.
limitations: Hardware: 16 GB (TRELLIS) to about 29 GB (Hunyuan3D 2.1 shape plus texture) of GPU memory, so player-side generation usually runs in the cloud or on high-end PCs.;Output topology and UVs are not authored for animation or LOD; production use still needs cleanup and review, which inZOI states it applies.;Generated assets are single objects without gameplay semantics; the game must assign function, footprint, and value.;Training data provenance and licenses vary by model, and player reception of generative AI can be negative (inZOI reviews in 2025).

name: LLM-written skill libraries (Voyager)
summary: An LLM agent that proposes its own next task, writes executable code to do it, refines the code from execution errors and self-checks, and stores verified programs in a retrievable skill library.
mechanism: Voyager drives a Minecraft bot through a JavaScript control API. An automatic curriculum asks GPT-4 for the next task given inventory, surroundings, and completed tasks, aiming to discover as many diverse things as possible. For each task GPT-4 writes a function that may call existing skills; the function runs, and the agent feeds back environment observations, execution errors, and a GPT-4 self-verification verdict, retrying up to four rounds before moving on. Verified functions are stored in a skill library indexed by an embedding of their description and retrieved (top-k) when writing later functions, so complex behaviors are composed from earlier ones. No model weights are trained; all learning is in the growing code library, which can be reused in a new world.
limitations: Depends on a frontier code model; GPT-3.5 produced 5.7x fewer items and GPT-4 cost 15x more per token, so per-agent cost is high.;Hallucinated tasks and calls: the curriculum proposed items that do not exist (copper sword), and generated code used invalid inputs or functions absent from the API, causing execution errors.;Self-verification misjudges success (for example not recognizing a dropped string as proof a spider was defeated).;Needs a scripting API that exposes game actions and state as text; it does not act from pixels.;Long-horizon factory building in Factorio still fails at multi-step automation and spatial layout.

name: Wave Function Collapse and constraint-based tile generation
summary: An example-driven constraint solver that fills a grid by repeatedly collapsing the lowest-entropy cell to one tile and propagating adjacency constraints, shipped in games including Townscaper, Bad North, and Caves of Qud.
mechanism: Each output cell starts with a domain of all tiles (simple tiled model) or of all N x N patterns extracted from one example image (overlapping model, typically N = 3). The solver repeatedly picks the undecided cell with the lowest Shannon entropy over its remaining options, a minimum-remaining-values heuristic, collapses it to one option sampled by that option's frequency in the example, and propagates: neighbors drop options that no longer have a compatible partner, which is arc consistency as in AC-3. If a domain empties, the attempt fails and the original algorithm restarts; later implementations add backtracking or local repair. Designers steer output with tile sets, adjacency rules, weights, pre-set cells, and extra global constraints. Townscaper runs it in real time on an irregular quad grid: the player toggles a cell's occupancy and the solver chooses compatible building modules from the surrounding shape, with decoration applied in a separate pass.
limitations: Only local adjacency is enforced; reachability, room counts, or path lengths need extra constraints, and Karth and Smith found a global constraint caused hundreds of conflicts that restarts could not clear within a minute.;Contradictions are possible because the underlying problem is NP-hard; shipped systems restart (Bad North) or accept silent local failures (Townscaper).;Interactive generation delay grows with structure size, and the overlapping model is slower and can copy the example too closely.;Quality depends on an authored module set, often hundreds of tiles (Bad North uses over 300), so art cost moves into modules rather than disappearing.
